questions.learningObjective: Compute buoyant force from submerged volume
questions.stem: A software ticket asks for the buoyant force on a 0.40 m^3 block fully submerged in water.

options.text: The buoyant force equals the weight of the 0.40 m^3 of water the block displaces.
The buoyant force equals the weight of the block itself regardless of displaced fluid.
options.misconception: confuses object weight with displaced fluid weight

options.text: The buoyant force is zero because the block is fully under the surface.
The buoyant force equals the block volume times its own density times g.
options.misconception: uses object density instead of fluid density

questions.explanation: Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid, so 0.40 m^3 of water sets the force. The block's own weight and density do not determine buoyancy.
questions.hint: Use displaced fluid weight, not object weight.

questions.topic: Apparent weight of a submerged block
questions.learningObjective: Compute apparent weight of a submerged block
questions.stem: A 60 N block is fully submerged in water and experiences 24 N of buoyant force.

options.text: The apparent weight of the block while submerged is 60 N because weight is unchanged.
options.misconception: ignores buoyant force in apparent weight

options.text: The apparent weight of the block while submerged is 36 N.
The apparent weight of the block while submerged is 84 N.
options.misconception: adds buoyant force instead of subtracting

options.text: The apparent weight of the block while submerged is 24 N.
options.misconception: confuses buoyant force with apparent weight

questions.explanation: Apparent weight is true weight minus buoyant force, so 60 N minus 24 N gives 36 N. Adding or ignoring the buoyant force gives wrong values.
questions.hint: Subtract buoyant force from true weight.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a light block floats
questions.stem: A wooden block of density 600 kg/m^3 is placed in water of density 1000 kg/m^3.

options.text: The block sinks because its density exceeds the density of water.
The block floats because its density is less than the density of water.
The block floats because wood is always lighter than any liquid.
options.misconception: overgeneralizes material instead of comparing densities

options.text: The block sinks because its mass is greater than the water mass.

questions.explanation: An object floats when its density is less than the fluid density, so 600 kg/m^3 wood floats in 1000 kg/m^3 water. Mass alone does not decide floating.
questions.hint: Compare object density to fluid density.

questions.stem: A solid sphere has the same density as the surrounding liquid and is fully submerged.

options.text: The sphere accelerates upward because buoyant force exceeds its weight.
The sphere accelerates downward because its weight exceeds buoyant force.
The sphere remains at rest at any depth because forces balance.
The sphere oscillates up and down because forces are unbalanced.

questions.explanation: Equal densities make weight equal buoyant force, so the sphere stays wherever placed. Neither force dominates, so no acceleration occurs.

questions.stem: A heavy box rests on a platform supported by a fluid column with no direct contact to the load.

options.text: The load cannot be supported because contact is required to transmit force.
The fluid pressure transmits the load upward through the column.
The load floats upward on its own because it is heavy.
The load disappears because pressure cancels all forces.
options.misconception: thinks pressure cancels rather than transmits

questions.explanation: Fluid pressure transmits force through the column even without direct contact. Contact is not the only way to support a load in a fluid.
questions.hint: Pressure can transmit force through fluid.

questions.stem: Squeezing a sealed bottle raises the pressure on a small diver inside it.

options.text: The diver sinks because increased pressure compresses its air and reduces displaced volume.
The diver rises because increased pressure pushes it upward.
options.misconception: confuses pressure increase with upward push

options.text: The diver stays still because the bottle is sealed.
The diver explodes because pressure always breaks small objects.

questions.explanation: Higher pressure compresses the trapped air, shrinking displaced volume and buoyant force, so the diver sinks. Pressure does not simply push the diver up.

questions.topic: Identifying a liquid from buoyant force data
questions.learningObjective: Identify liquid density from buoyant force
questions.stem: A 0.10 m^3 block fully submerged experiences 980 N of buoyant force; find the liquid density (g=9.8).
questions.explanation: Density equals buoyant force divided by volume times g: 980/(0.10*9.8)=100 kg/m^3. The arithmetic gives the liquid density directly.

questions.stem: A student measures a submerged stone and records a smaller scale reading than in air.

options.text: The reading is smaller because the stone's mass decreased underwater.
The reading is smaller because buoyancy reduces the apparent weight.
The reading is smaller because gravity weakens underwater.
The reading is smaller because water dissolves the stone.

questions.explanation: Mass and gravity are unchanged, but buoyancy opposes weight, reducing apparent weight. The scale reads the net downward force.

questions.stem: A fully submerged object is lowered deeper in an incompressible liquid.

options.text: Buoyant force increases because pressure is greater at depth.
Buoyant force decreases because the object is compressed.
Buoyant force stays the same because displaced volume is unchanged.
Buoyant force becomes zero because pressure balances everywhere.

questions.explanation: For an incompressible fluid and rigid object, displaced volume does not change with depth, so buoyant force stays constant. Pressure changes but net buoyancy does not.

questions.stem: Water flows through a pipe whose cross-sectional area halves from 0.04 m^2 to 0.02 m^2.

options.text: The flow speed halves in the narrower section.
The flow speed doubles in the narrower section.
The flow speed stays the same because the fluid is incompressible.
The flow speed quadruples because area is squared.

questions.explanation: Continuity requires A1 v1 = A2 v2, so halving area doubles speed. Speed and area are inversely proportional.

questions.learningObjective: Compute buoyant force with different fluid
questions.stem: A 0.25 m^3 block is fully submerged in oil of density 800 kg/m^3 (g=9.8).

options.text: Buoyant force is 0.25*800*9.8 = 1960 N.
Buoyant force is 0.25*1000*9.8 = 2450 N.
Buoyant force is 0.25*800*1.0 = 200 N.
Buoyant force is 800/0.25*9.8 = 31360 N.

questions.explanation: Buoyant force is fluid density times submerged volume times g, so 800*0.25*9.8 = 1960 N. Using water density or omitting g is wrong.
questions.hint: Multiply fluid density, volume, and g.

questions.topic: Apparent weight of a submerged block
questions.stem: A 90 N block is fully submerged and displaced 0.005 m^3 of water (g=9.8).

options.text: Apparent weight is 90 - 0.005*1000*9.8 = 41 N.
Apparent weight is 90 + 0.005*1000*9.8 = 139 N.
Apparent weight is 90 - 0.005*90 = 89.55 N.

options.misconception: uses block weight as fluid density

options.text: Apparent weight is 0.005*1000*9.8 = 49 N.

options.misconception: reports buoyant force as apparent weight

questions.explanation: Apparent weight equals 90 N minus buoyant force 0.005*1000*9.8 = 49 N, giving 41 N. Adding or miscomputing gives wrong results.

questions.learningObjective: Predict float or sink from densities
questions.stem: A block of density 1200 kg/m^3 is placed in water of density 1000 kg/m^3.

options.text: It floats because its density is close to water density.
It sinks because its density exceeds water density.
It floats because 1200 is larger than 1000.
It neither floats nor sinks because densities differ.

questions.explanation: An object sinks when its density exceeds fluid density, so 1200 kg/m^3 sinks in 1000 kg/m^3 water. Closeness does not cause floating.
questions.hint: Sink if object density exceeds fluid density.

questions.stem: A block of mass 2.0 kg and volume 0.002 m^3 is neutrally buoyant in a liquid (g=9.8).
questions.explanation: Neutral buoyancy requires object density equal liquid density: 2.0/0.002 = 1000 kg/m^3. The liquid density must match.

questions.stem: A fluid-filled glove transmits a push from one finger to another without touching.

options.text: The push travels because fluid pressure changes spread through the glove.
The push travels because the glove material stretches.
The push cannot travel because the fingers do not touch.
The push travels because air inside the glove carries it.

options.misconception: invokes air instead of fluid pressure

questions.explanation: Fluid pressure changes propagate through the fluid, transmitting force without direct contact. Material stretch or air is not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A diver at rest is squeezed harder while the bottle remains sealed.

options.text: It rises because squeezing pushes water out of the diver.
It sinks deeper because trapped air compresses further.
It stays at the same depth because the bottle is sealed.
It breaks because pressure always destroys small objects.

questions.explanation: More squeezing raises pressure, compressing trapped air further and reducing buoyancy, so the diver sinks deeper. Sealing does not prevent compression.

questions.topic: Identifying a liquid from buoyant force data
questions.stem: A 0.05 m^3 submerged block experiences 490 N buoyant force (g=9.8).

options.text: Liquid density is 490/(0.05*9.8)=1000 kg/m^3.
Liquid density is 0.05*9.8/490=0.001 kg/m^3.
Liquid density is 490*0.05*9.8=239.9 kg/m^3.
Liquid density is 490/0.05=9800 kg/m^3.

questions.explanation: Density equals buoyant force over volume times g: 490/(0.05*9.8)=1000 kg/m^3. Inverting or omitting g is wrong.
questions.hint: Divide by Vg, not just V.

questions.stem: A 50 N stone submerged in water displaces 0.003 m^3 of water (g=9.8).

options.text: Scale reads 50 N because weight is invariant.

questions.explanation: Apparent weight is 50 N minus buoyant force 0.003*1000*9.8 = 29.4 N, giving 20.6 N. Weight itself is unchanged but apparent weight drops.

questions.stem: A student claims buoyant force grows with depth because water pressure increases.

options.text: The claim is correct because pressure increases with depth.
The claim is wrong because buoyant force depends only on displaced volume.
The claim is wrong because gravity decreases with depth.
The claim is correct because pressure differences vanish at depth.

questions.explanation: Buoyant force depends on displaced volume, not depth, for an incompressible fluid. Pressure increases but the net pressure difference stays tied to volume.

questions.stem: Water at 2 m/s flows through a pipe area 0.06 m^2 into area 0.02 m^2.

options.text: New speed is 2*0.06/0.02 = 6 m/s.
New speed is 2*0.02/0.06 = 0.67 m/s.
New speed is 2 + 0.06 - 0.02 = 2.04 m/s.

questions.explanation: Continuity gives v2 = v1*A1/A2 = 2*0.06/0.02 = 6 m/s. Inverting or combining areas incorrectly is wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Compute buoyant force on irregular shape
questions.stem: An irregular object displaces 0.08 m^3 of seawater of density 1025 kg/m^3 (g=9.8).
questions.explanation: Buoyant force is 1025*0.08*9.8 = 803.6 N. Shape does not matter, only displaced volume.

questions.topic: Apparent weight of a submerged block
questions.stem: A heavy anchor feels lighter when lifted through water than through air.

options.text: It feels lighter because water buoyancy opposes its weight.
It feels lighter because water reduces the anchor's mass.
It feels lighter because gravity is weaker in water.
It feels lighter because water dissolves part of the anchor.

questions.explanation: Buoyancy opposes weight in water, reducing apparent weight. Mass and gravity are unchanged.

questions.stem: A plastic cube of density 900 kg/m^3 floats in water of density 1000 kg/m^3.

options.text: It floats because its density is less than water density.
It floats because plastic is always light.
It floats because its mass is small.
It floats because water pushes only light objects.

questions.explanation: Floating occurs when object density is less than fluid density. Material name or mass alone does not decide.

questions.stem: A submerged submarine adjusts its ballast so its overall density equals seawater density.

options.text: It will accelerate upward because buoyancy exceeds weight.
It will accelerate downward because weight exceeds buoyancy.
It will remain at constant depth because forces balance.
It will bob up and down because forces are equal.

questions.explanation: Equal densities balance weight and buoyancy, so the submarine stays at constant depth. Balanced forces mean no acceleration.

questions.stem: A 100 N load on a 0.05 m^2 piston transmits pressure to a 0.02 m^2 piston.

options.text: Transmitted pressure is 100/0.05 = 2000 Pa.
Transmitted pressure is 100/0.02 = 5000 Pa.
Transmitted pressure is 100*0.05 = 5 Pa.
Transmitted pressure is 0 because pistons do not touch.

questions.explanation: Pressure equals force over input area: 100/0.05 = 2000 Pa, transmitted through fluid. Contact is unnecessary.

questions.stem: Releasing the squeeze lets a sunken diver return toward the surface.

options.text: It rises because trapped air expands and increases displaced volume.
It rises because pressure pushes it upward.
It rises because water leaves the diver.
It stays sunk because the bottle is sealed.

questions.explanation: Releasing squeeze lowers pressure, expanding trapped air and increasing displaced volume and buoyancy, so the diver rises. Pressure itself does not push it up.

questions.topic: Identifying a liquid from buoyant force data
questions.stem: A 0.02 m^3 block experiences 156.8 N buoyant force (g=9.8).

options.text: Liquid density is 156.8/(0.02*9.8)=800 kg/m^3.
Liquid density is 0.02*9.8/156.8=0.00125 kg/m^3.
Liquid density is 156.8*0.02*9.8=30.7 kg/m^3.
Liquid density is 156.8/0.02=7840 kg/m^3.

questions.explanation: Density equals 156.8/(0.02*9.8)=800 kg/m^3. The liquid could be oil. Inverting or omitting g is wrong.

questions.stem: A submerged object shows apparent weight 30 N and buoyant force 20 N; find true weight.
questions.explanation: True weight equals apparent weight plus buoyant force: 30 + 20 = 50 N. The buoyant force must be added back.
questions.hint: Add buoyant force to apparent weight.

questions.stem: A diver descends in a lake and notices pressure on her increases.

options.text: Pressure increases because the water column above her grows taller.
Pressure increases because gravity strengthens with depth.
Pressure decreases because water spreads out.
Pressure is unchanged because water is incompressible.

questions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure increases with depth due to the weight of the overlying fluid column. Gravity and incompressibility do not change this.
questions.hint: Taller water column means more pressure.

questions.stem: A river narrows between two banks and the water speeds up.

options.text: Speed increases because the same flow rate passes through less area.
Speed increases because the river pushes harder.
Speed decreases because narrowing blocks the flow.
Speed stays the same because water volume is conserved.

questions.explanation: Continuity keeps flow rate constant, so narrower area means higher speed. Push or volume conservation alone is insufficient.

questions.stem: Two identical volumes are submerged, one in water and one in mercury.

options.text: Buoyant force is greater in mercury because mercury is denser.
Buoyant force is greater in water because water is lighter.
Buoyant forces are equal because volumes are equal.
Buoyant force is zero in both because they are submerged.

questions.explanation: Buoyant force equals fluid density times volume times g, so denser mercury gives larger buoyancy. Equal volumes alone do not imply equal forces.

questions.topic: Apparent weight of a submerged block
questions.stem: A 40 N block is fully submerged in oil; displaced oil weighs 12 N.

options.text: Apparent weight is 40 - 12 = 28 N.
Apparent weight is 40 + 12 = 52 N.
Apparent weight is 12 N.
Apparent weight is 40 N because oil is not water.

questions.explanation: Apparent weight is true weight minus buoyant force: 40 - 12 = 28 N. Any fluid provides buoyancy.

questions.stem: A floating block rests with only part of its volume below the surface.

options.text: It floats with partial submersion because displaced water weight equals block weight.
It floats with partial submersion because the block is light.
It sinks partially because gravity pulls only part of it.
It floats fully submerged because partial is unstable.

questions.explanation: Floating equilibrium requires buoyant force, from displaced water, to equal block weight, which occurs at partial submersion. 'Light' alone is imprecise.
questions.hint: Displaced water weight equals block weight.

questions.stem: A 3.0 kg object must be neutrally buoyant in water (density 1000 kg/m^3).

options.text: Required volume is 3.0/1000 = 0.003 m^3.
Required volume is 1000/3.0 = 333 m^3.
Required volume is 3.0*1000 = 3000 m^3.
Required volume is 3.0*9.8 = 29.4 m^3.

questions.explanation: Neutral buoyancy requires object density equal water density, so volume = mass/density = 3.0/1000 = 0.003 m^3. Inverting or multiplying is wrong.

questions.stem: A fluid transmits 500 Pa pressure from a small piston to a large piston.
questions.explanation: Pascal's principle says pressure is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid, so the large piston sees 500 Pa. Pressure, not force, is transmitted equally.

questions.stem: A Cartesian diver floats at mid-depth before any squeeze is applied.

options.text: It floats at mid-depth because its density equals water density.
It floats at mid-depth because it is light.
It floats at mid-depth because pressure is zero.
It floats at mid-depth because gravity is balanced by air.

questions.explanation: At mid-depth the diver's average density equals water density, so forces balance. 'Light' alone does not explain the depth.

questions.topic: Identifying a liquid from buoyant force data
questions.stem: Computed liquid density from buoyancy data is 13600 kg/m^3.

options.text: The liquid is likely mercury because mercury is very dense.
The liquid is likely water because water is common.
The liquid is likely oil because oil floats.
The liquid is likely air because 13600 is small.

questions.explanation: A density of 13600 kg/m^3 matches mercury, much denser than water or oil. Commonness does not override the computed value.

questions.stem: An object's mass is 5 kg and it is submerged in water.

options.text: Its mass remains 5 kg underwater because mass is invariant.
Its mass decreases underwater because water supports it.
Its mass increases underwater because water adds mass.
Its mass becomes zero underwater because it floats.

questions.explanation: Mass is an intrinsic property and does not change with location or submersion. Support affects apparent weight, not mass.

questions.stem: A rigid 0.1 m^3 block is submerged 10 m deep in water (g=9.8).

options.text: Buoyant force is 0.1*1000*9.8 = 980 N regardless of depth.
Buoyant force is 0.1*1000*9.8*10 = 9800 N.
Buoyant force is 0.1*10*9.8 = 9.8 N.
Buoyant force is zero because pressure balances at depth.

questions.explanation: Buoyant force depends on displaced volume, not depth, so it is 980 N. Multiplying by depth is incorrect.

questions.stem: Water flows at 3 m/s through a pipe of area 0.05 m^2.

options.text: Flow rate is 3*0.05 = 0.15 m^3/s.
Flow rate is 3/0.05 = 60 m^3/s.
Flow rate is 3+0.05 = 3.05 m^3/s.
Flow rate is 0.05/3 = 0.0167 m^3/s.

questions.explanation: Flow rate equals speed times area: 3*0.05 = 0.15 m^3/s. Dividing or adding is wrong.

questions.stem: A 0.15 m^3 block is submerged in alcohol of density 790 kg/m^3 (g=9.8).

options.text: Buoyant force is 790*0.15*9.8 = 1161.3 N.
Buoyant force is 1000*0.15*9.8 = 1470 N.
Buoyant force is 790*0.15 = 118.5 N.
Buoyant force is 790/0.15*9.8 = 51546.7 N.

questions.explanation: Buoyant force is 790*0.15*9.8 = 1161.3 N. Using water density or omitting g is wrong.

questions.topic: Apparent weight of a submerged block
questions.stem: A 120 N block submerged in water has volume 0.01 m^3 (g=9.8, water density 1000).
questions.explanation: Buoyant force is 0.01*1000*9.8 = 98 N, so apparent weight is 120 - 98 = 22 N. The arithmetic checks out.

questions.stem: A block of density 500 kg/m^3 is dropped into water of density 1000 kg/m^3.

options.text: It floats because its density is half the water density.
It sinks because 500 is less than 1000.
It floats because 500 is a small number.
It sinks because its mass is too small.

questions.explanation: The block floats because 500 kg/m^3 is less than 1000 kg/m^3. The comparison, not the absolute value, decides.

questions.stem: A neutrally buoyant object is pushed slightly deeper in a uniform liquid.

options.text: It stays at the new depth because forces still balance.
It rises back because buoyancy increases with depth.
It sinks further because weight increases with depth.
It oscillates forever because forces are equal.

questions.explanation: At neutral buoyancy forces balance at any depth in a uniform liquid, so the object stays where pushed. Neither force changes with depth.

questions.stem: A platform is held up by fluid pressure with no solid link to the load above.

options.text: The load is supported because fluid pressure pushes upward on the platform.
The load is unsupported because no solid link exists.
The load floats away because fluid pushes it up.
The load vanishes because pressure cancels weight.

questions.explanation: Fluid pressure can support a load without a solid link by pushing upward on the platform. Contact is not required.

questions.stem: A diver floats near the top; the bottle is squeezed slightly.

options.text: It sinks a little because air compresses and buoyancy drops.
It rises because squeezing pushes it up.
It stays because the bottle is sealed.
It breaks because pressure always destroys small objects.

questions.explanation: Squeezing raises pressure, compressing air and reducing buoyancy, so the diver sinks. Sealing does not prevent compression.

questions.topic: Identifying a liquid from buoyant force data
questions.stem: A 0.04 m^3 block experiences 313.6 N buoyant force (g=9.8).

options.text: Liquid density is 313.6/(0.04*9.8)=800 kg/m^3.
Liquid density is 0.04*9.8/313.6=0.00125 kg/m^3.
Liquid density is 313.6*0.04*9.8=123.0 kg/m^3.
Liquid density is 313.6/0.04=7840 kg/m^3.

questions.explanation: Density equals 313.6/(0.04*9.8)=800 kg/m^3. Inverting or omitting g is wrong.

questions.stem: A stone weighs 80 N in air and 50 N when submerged in water.

options.text: Buoyant force is 80 - 50 = 30 N.
Buoyant force is 80 + 50 = 130 N.
Buoyant force is 50 N.
Buoyant force is 80 N.

questions.explanation: Buoyant force equals the loss of apparent weight: 80 - 50 = 30 N. Adding or picking one weight is wrong.

questions.stem: A block's volume changes by 1% due to pressure at 100 m depth; buoyancy changes by about 1%.
questions.explanation: If volume changes 1%, buoyant force changes about 1% because force is proportional to displaced volume. The value is a small percentage.

questions.stem: A pipe area 0.1 m^2 carries water at 1 m/s into area 0.025 m^2.

options.text: Speed becomes 1*0.1/0.025 = 4 m/s.
Speed becomes 1*0.025/0.1 = 0.25 m/s.
Speed becomes 1+0.1-0.025 = 1.075 m/s.
Speed becomes 1*0.1*0.025 = 0.0025 m/s.

questions.explanation: Continuity gives v2 = 1*0.1/0.025 = 4 m/s. Inverting or combining areas is wrong.

questions.stem: A floating block displaces 0.03 m^3 of water (density 1000 kg/m^3, g=9.8).

options.text: Buoyant force is 0.03*1000*9.8 = 294 N.
Buoyant force is 0.03*1000 = 30 N.
Buoyant force is 0.03*9.8 = 0.294 N.

questions.explanation: Buoyant force is 0.03*1000*9.8 = 294 N. Omitting g or dividing volume is wrong.

questions.topic: Apparent weight of a submerged block
questions.stem: An object's apparent weight underwater is zero.

options.text: Buoyant force equals the object's weight, so it is neutrally buoyant.
The object has no mass underwater.
Gravity stops acting underwater.
Water dissolves the object completely.

questions.explanation: Zero apparent weight means buoyant force equals weight, so the object is neutrally buoyant. Mass and gravity are unchanged.

questions.stem: A block of density 400 kg/m^3 floats in water of density 1000 kg/m^3.

options.text: Fraction submerged is 400/1000 = 0.4.
Fraction submerged is 1000/400 = 2.5.
Fraction submerged is 400*1000 = 400000.
Fraction submerged is 1 - 400/1000 = 0.6.

questions.explanation: For a floating object, fraction submerged equals object density over fluid density: 400/1000 = 0.4. Inverting or using exposed fraction is wrong.
questions.hint: Divide object density by fluid density.

questions.stem: A student says a neutrally buoyant object will rise if pushed down.

options.text: That is wrong because forces remain balanced at the new depth.
That is right because buoyancy increases with depth.
That is right because weight decreases with depth.
That is wrong because gravity stops at depth.

questions.explanation: In a uniform liquid, buoyant force does not change with depth for a rigid object, so forces stay balanced. The object remains at the new depth.

questions.stem: Pressure 2000 Pa acts on a 0.03 m^2 output piston.

options.text: Output force is 2000*0.03 = 60 N.
Output force is 2000/0.03 = 66666.7 N.
Output force is 2000+0.03 = 2000.03 N.
Output force is 0 because pistons do not touch.

questions.explanation: Force equals pressure times area: 2000*0.03 = 60 N. Dividing or adding is wrong, and contact is not required.

questions.stem: Trapped air volume halves when bottle pressure doubles; buoyant force halves.
questions.explanation: If displaced volume halves, buoyant force halves because force is proportional to volume. The factor is 0.5.

questions.topic: Identifying a liquid from buoyant force data
questions.stem: An object floats higher in liquid X than in water.

options.text: Liquid X is denser than water because less volume is displaced.
Liquid X is less dense than water because the object floats.
Liquid X has the same density as water.
Liquid X is lighter because the object rises.

questions.explanation: Floating higher means less displaced volume, which requires denser fluid to provide the same buoyant force. Less dense fluid would sink the object more.

questions.stem: An object has mass 10 kg; find its weight in air (g=9.8).

options.text: Weight is 10*9.8 = 98 N.
Weight is 10/9.8 = 1.02 kg.
Weight is 10 + 9.8 = 19.8 N.
Weight is 10 N because mass equals weight.

questions.explanation: Weight equals mass times g: 10*9.8 = 98 N. Dividing or adding is wrong, and mass is not weight.

questions.stem: A student says a submarine's buoyant force is larger at 100 m than at 10 m.

options.text: That is false because displaced volume and fluid density are unchanged.
That is true because pressure is larger at 100 m.
That is true because water is denser at depth.
That is false because gravity is weaker at depth.

questions.explanation: For an incompressible fluid, buoyant force depends on displaced volume and density, neither of which changes with depth. Pressure alone does not change buoyancy.

questions.stem: Water flows at 2 m/s through area 0.08 m^2; find area for speed 4 m/s.
questions.explanation: Continuity gives A2 = A1*v1/v2 = 0.08*2/4 = 0.04 m^2. Inverting or adding is wrong.
